title: Nutmeg and Pebble's Great Bell Rescue
markdown:
Meadowbrook dressed itself for the Harvest Parade: flags, ribbons, the smell of cinnamon buns. Nutmeg the squirrel loved the colour and dreaded the brass. Crowds sent shivers down his bushy tail. His whiskers twitched faster than was strictly needed.

He was the forest’s champion acorn-finder. His best pal, Pebble the pony, was steady and cheerful, hooves that liked to trot, eyes that promised adventure and old stories about brave ancestors.

One sun-drenched afternoon Siwan, the village elder, a kind man whose white beard seemed to keep extra secrets, looked worried. “The parade cannot begin without the Great Bell. Vanished. Gone.”

His eyes caught the soft mud. “Old hoofprints. Faint. They lead away from the village. You two are quick and clever. Will you find the bell before we start?”

Nutmeg’s tail drooped. Strange noises. New places. He imagined thunder instead of drums. Pebble nudged him with a soft nose. “Come on. An adventure. Our ancestors would have jumped.”

They set off, Pebble in a calm rhythm, Nutmeg darting to trace the prints.

The Whispering Woods leaned in like gossip. Leaves rustled in two voices at once. Shadows practised being monsters, then forgot their lines and became only shade. Nutmeg’s heart thumped like a moth in a jar. A twig cracked behind them; it was only Pebble. “Are you sure this is the way?”

Pebble chuckled, a rumble. “The prints are still here. A little forest mystery.” He paused so Nutmeg could sniff a print that held a crescent of mud and a smell of old iron, as if the bell had already breathed on the path.

Next came the Giggling Stream, bubbling over mossy stones that looked pleased with themselves. A fallen log, slick with dew, lay across it. Nutmeg zipped, then turned to watch. Pebble, heavier, took his time. Hooves found steady spots. The log wobbled and sent a necklace of drops into the chuckle. Nutmeg held his breath. “Careful.” Pebble kept his eyes ahead, one hoof, then the next, until the far bank accepted him.

Near a mossy boulder a grumpy badger, polishing his glasses, grumbled a riddle scratched in the stone. “I have a tongue, but cannot speak. I have a mouth, but cannot eat. What am I?”

Nutmeg’s mind whirred. Pebble stamped. “A shoe,” Nutmeg shouted, face lighting. The badger grunted and pointed down the path. Under prickly bushes: a hollow log that smelled of rain and hiding. Inside, in dappled light, the Great Bell. Cool old metal, a dent like a smile. They nearly cheered, then remembered the woods like secrets kept, and cheered with their eyes instead.

Then a low rumble from far away: the band tuning. A fierce gust whipped leaves into a dance. The hoofprints vanished under swirling green.

Lost. The bell heavy as lead. The rumble grew. Nutmeg wanted to burrow and disappear. Not brave enough, said a small inner voice. Pebble’s nose was a warm anchor. “We’re together. The village needs us.”

Nutmeg thought of storms in Pebble’s stories, of the square without its note. He looked at the bell, then at hopeful pony eyes. “Let’s go. We have to be fast.”

He scrambled onto Pebble’s back, the bell tight in his paws, the clapper held still with a thumb so it would not ring too soon and spend itself in the trees. Pebble galloped. Roots tried to argue. Nutmeg pointed left, then low. The parade noise rose, a brass weather they were running toward on purpose. Green and brown rushed past. Once Pebble slipped on wet leaves; Nutmeg leaned, and they did not fall.

They burst from the trees on the first bold drum. Cheers. Siwan rushed forward, beaming. “The bell. You found it.” Nutmeg, still a little shaky, placed it in Siwan’s hands. Pebble panted, proud. The Great Bell rang, clear and joyful, and the best Harvest Parade Meadowbrook had yet seen began on time.

Nutmeg stood beside Pebble while the brass, at last, was a sound he had brought home. He did not call it magic. He only stayed in the square, tail still, and let the next cheer find him.
